questions.stem: This graph plots airway resistance against lung volume, with insets showing airway caliber at low versus high lung volumes. What relationship and mechanism does it illustrate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Resistance falls as lung volume rises because radial traction from surrounding alveoli widens the airways

choices.label: B
choices.text: Resistance is independent of lung volume

choices.label: C
choices.text: Resistance is lowest at residual volume and highest at total lung capacity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Resistance rises as lung volume rises because expanding alveoli compress the airways

choices.label: E
choices.text: Resistance falls as lung volume rises because of bronchial smooth-muscle contraction

explanation.summary: Airway resistance is inversely related to lung volume. At high lung volumes, the surrounding distended alveoli exert outward radial traction on the airway walls, holding them open and lowering resistance; at low lung volumes this tethering is lost and small airways narrow, raising resistance.
explanation.whyCorrect: Airway resistance is inversely related to lung volume. At high lung volumes, the surrounding distended alveoli exert outward radial traction on the airway walls, holding them open and lowering resistance; at low lung volumes this tethering is lost and small airways narrow, raising resistance.

questions.stem: Panel A contrasts a normal lung with an emphysematous lung during forced expiration and marks the equal pressure point (EPP); panel C shows a scooped-out expiratory flow-volume loop. In emphysema, why does forced expiration cause premature airway collapse?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increased elastic recoil pulls the airways shut

choices.label: B
choices.text: Loss of elastic recoil and radial traction shifts the equal pressure point into small, non-cartilaginous airways

choices.label: C
choices.text: Surfactant deficiency collapses the alveoli directly

choices.label: D
choices.text: Excess mucus plugs the large cartilaginous airways

choices.label: E
choices.text: Bronchial smooth-muscle hypertrophy actively narrows the airways

explanation.summary: Emphysema destroys alveolar walls, reducing elastic recoil and the radial traction that tethers small airways open. During forced expiration the equal pressure point (where intraluminal pressure equals pleural pressure) moves upstream into airways lacking cartilage, which collapse and limit flow, producing the scooped-out (concave) expiratory flow-volume loop of obstructive disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Emphysema destroys alveolar walls, reducing elastic recoil and the radial traction that tethers small airways open. During forced expiration the equal pressure point (where intraluminal pressure equals pleural pressure) moves upstream into airways lacking cartilage, which collapse and limit flow, producing the scooped-out (concave) expiratory flow-volume loop of obstructive disease.

questions.stem: This pressure-volume curve of the lung shows hysteresis loops (A, B, C) tidal-breathing around three different starting volumes. Around which point does a given change in pressure produce the LARGEST change in volume?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Point C, near total lung capacity (high FRC)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Point B, near normal FRC

choices.label: C
choices.text: Compliance is identical at A, B and C

choices.label: D
choices.text: Point A, near residual volume (low FRC)

choices.label: E
choices.text: At the very top of the curve at TLC

explanation.summary: Compliance (ΔV/ΔP, the slope) is greatest along the steep middle of the pressure-volume curve near normal FRC (B). At low volumes (A, atelectasis) and high volumes (C, overexpansion) the curve flattens, so the lung is stiffer and more work is needed for the same volume change.
explanation.whyCorrect: Compliance (ΔV/ΔP, the slope) is greatest along the steep middle of the pressure-volume curve near normal FRC (B). At low volumes (A, atelectasis) and high volumes (C, overexpansion) the curve flattens, so the lung is stiffer and more work is needed for the same volume change.

questions.stem: This graph plots lung, chest wall, and combined respiratory-system recoil against distending pressure. What does the point where the respiratory-system curve crosses zero pressure (at FRC) represent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The point of airway collapse and total emptying (RV)

choices.label: B
choices.text: The volume of maximal inspiratory effort (TLC)

choices.label: C
choices.text: The volume where airway resistance is lowest

choices.label: D
choices.text: The point where lung and chest wall compliance are both zero

choices.label: E
choices.text: The volume where inward lung recoil exactly balances outward chest wall recoil

explanation.summary: At functional residual capacity the lung's inward elastic recoil is exactly opposed by the chest wall's outward recoil, so the net (respiratory-system) recoil pressure is zero and no muscular effort is required to hold this volume. This is the resting end-expiratory position.
explanation.whyCorrect: At functional residual capacity the lung's inward elastic recoil is exactly opposed by the chest wall's outward recoil, so the net (respiratory-system) recoil pressure is zero and no muscular effort is required to hold this volume. This is the resting end-expiratory position.

questions.stem: This figure shows how the lung compliance curve shifts (dashed lines) and the resulting change in resting lung volume. An increase in lung compliance, as seen in emphysema, produces which change in FRC?

choices.label: A
choices.text: FRC increases, because the more compliant lung recoils inward less

choices.label: B
choices.text: FRC decreases, because inward recoil overwhelms the chest wall

choices.label: C
choices.text: FRC becomes equal to total lung capacity

choices.label: D
choices.text: FRC falls to residual volume

choices.label: E
choices.text: FRC is unchanged, since chest wall recoil alone sets it

explanation.summary: Raising lung compliance (loss of elastic tissue in emphysema) weakens inward lung recoil. The balance point with the outward chest wall recoil then shifts to a higher volume, raising FRC and producing hyperinflation. Reduced compliance (fibrosis) does the opposite and lowers FRC.
explanation.whyCorrect: Raising lung compliance (loss of elastic tissue in emphysema) weakens inward lung recoil. The balance point with the outward chest wall recoil then shifts to a higher volume, raising FRC and producing hyperinflation. Reduced compliance (fibrosis) does the opposite and lowers FRC.

questions.stem: These two tubes differ only in radius (r), with the same driving pressure. Based on Poiseuille's law, halving the radius of an airway changes its resistance by what factor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Resistance doubles

choices.label: B
choices.text: Resistance is unchanged

choices.label: C
choices.text: Resistance increases 8-fold

choices.label: D
choices.text: Resistance increases 16-fold

choices.label: E
choices.text: Resistance increases 4-fold

explanation.summary: For laminar flow, resistance is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the radius (R ∝ 1/r⁴). Halving r multiplies resistance by 2⁴ = 16. This is why small changes in airway caliber (e.g., bronchoconstriction) have dramatic effects on airflow.
explanation.whyCorrect: For laminar flow, resistance is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the radius (R ∝ 1/r⁴). Halving r multiplies resistance by 2⁴ = 16. This is why small changes in airway caliber (e.g., bronchoconstriction) have dramatic effects on airflow.

questions.stem: The left graph shows airway resistance peaking at medium-sized (segmental) bronchi and falling in the small airways; the right graph shows total cross-sectional area rising steeply in later generations. Why is resistance LOWEST in the smallest, most distal airways despite their tiny individual diameters?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Air becomes fully turbulent and flows faster there

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are arranged in massive parallel numbers

choices.label: C
choices.text: Surfactant eliminates all resistance in small airways

choices.label: D
choices.text: The alveoli actively pump air to reduce resistance

choices.label: E
choices.text: Each small airway individually has a very large radius

explanation.summary: Resistances in parallel add reciprocally, so the vast number of small airways branching in parallel gives a huge total cross-sectional area and a very low combined resistance. Medium bronchi contribute most airway resistance because their total cross-sectional area is comparatively small.
explanation.whyCorrect: Resistances in parallel add reciprocally, so the vast number of small airways branching in parallel gives a huge total cross-sectional area and a very low combined resistance. Medium bronchi contribute most airway resistance because their total cross-sectional area is comparatively small.

questions.stem: This diagram contrasts two patterns of gas flow through a tube (smooth parallel streamlines above, chaotic swirling below). Which factor most favors the transition from the upper pattern to the lower, disordered pattern?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A lower flow velocity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased gas viscosity

choices.label: C
choices.text: A high Reynolds number

choices.label: D
choices.text: Decreased gas density (e.g., breathing heliox)

choices.label: E
choices.text: A narrower, unbranched airway

explanation.summary: The upper pattern is laminar and the lower is turbulent flow. Turbulence develops when the Reynolds number is high, which is favored by high velocity, high gas density, and large diameter, and opposed by high viscosity. Turbulent flow makes pressure proportional to the square of flow, raising the work of breathing.
explanation.whyCorrect: The upper pattern is laminar and the lower is turbulent flow. Turbulence develops when the Reynolds number is high, which is favored by high velocity, high gas density, and large diameter, and opposed by high viscosity. Turbulent flow makes pressure proportional to the square of flow, raising the work of breathing.
